author: Grace Hall
title: Trump's Plan for More Cuts Without Congress' Approval - NewsBreak
text: The White House is reportedly weighing pocket rescissions to enact major spending cuts without Congress, aiming for billions in reductions flagged by the Department of Government Efficiency. Key Republicans have questioned the method’s legality and practicality. Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought has supported pocket rescissions, citing President Ford’s precedent and defending its legality despite past failures, including President Donald Trump’s $15 billion attempt. Vought said, “The very Impoundment Control Act itself allows for a procedure called pocket rescissions, later in the year, to be able to bank some of these savings, without the bill actually being passed. It’s a provision that has been rarely used. But it is there. And we intend to use all of these tools.” Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) questioned the viability of the $9.4 billion rescissions package. Under the Impoundment Control Act (ICA), pocket rescissions occur when requests are made with under 45 days left in the fiscal year, allowing unspent funds to expire without a Congressional vote. Collins said, “Pocket rescissions are illegal, in my judgment, and contradict the will of Congress and the constitutional authority of Congress to appropriate funds.” Experts warned that pocket rescissions could face legal challenges. The GAO suggests the ICA may not permit withholding funds until expiration. However, some legal scholars note the ICA doesn’t explicitly ban the practice, leaving room for interpretation. Heritage Foundation Legal Fellow Jack Fitzhenry said, “[The GAO report] is not a bad piece of legal work, but it doesn’t strike me as a lockdown answer to the question. It essentially requires whoever is interpreting [the ICA] to read into the language a limitation that is not there, that Congress did not bother to put into the statute.” Failure by Sen. Collins to hold a vote could sink the rescission package. Lawmakers remain wary of pocket rescissions’ impact on the balance of power between Congress and the executive branch. Grace Hall covers U.S. politics & news for content partner Modern Newsstand LLC.
